claims.evidence: Original: "Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used for ..." | Retrieved: NHS: immunosuppressant prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis (incl. psoriatic arthritis), Crohn's disease; can also be prescribed for cancer.
claims.newSentence: Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease, and sometimes for cancer.

claims.evidence: Original: "When it is used for arthritis and similar conditions, methotrexate is taken once a week, not every day." | Retrieved: MHRA Drug Safety Update (Sept 2020): once-weekly dosing for autoimmune diseases; risk of fatal overdose from inadvertent daily dosing. NHS: dosing is weekly not daily. MedlinePlus: some people who took it daily instead of weekly died.
claims.newSentence: When it is used for autoimmune conditions such as these, it is taken once a week, not every day.

claims.evidence: Original: "Taking it daily by mistake instead of weekly has led to overdoses that were sometimes fatal." | Retrieved: MHRA: accidental daily instead of weekly dosing has caused fatal overdose; MedlinePlus: some people died.
claims.newSentence: Taking it daily by mistake instead of weekly has caused overdoses that were sometimes fatal.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says anyone who thinks they have taken too much methotrexate should seek advice from the prescriber or NHS 111 straight away." | Retrieved: NHS how-and-when page: contact 111 right away if more than the prescribed amount was taken or it was taken daily instead of weekly. MHRA: seek medical advice promptly if overdose suspected.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 right away if more methotrexate than prescribed has been taken, including taking it daily instead of weekly.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says it calms the immune system to help stop it attacking the body's own cells." | Retrieved: NHS: slows down/calms the immune system and reduces inflammation.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says it calms the immune system and helps reduce inflammation.

claims.evidence: Original: "Methotrexate blocks an enzyme called dihydrofolate reductase, which the body needs to make tetrahydrofolate, the active form of folic acid. Tetrahydrofolate is needed to build the nucleotides of DNA and RNA." | Retrieved: Review abstracts: polyglutamated methotrexate inhibits DHFR, decreasing tetrahydrofolate production, which inhibits DNA, RNA and protein synthesis.
claims.newSentence: Methotrexate blocks an enzyme called dihydrofolate reductase, which the body uses to make tetrahydrofolate, a form of folate needed to build DNA and RNA.

claims.evidence: Original: "In inflammatory conditions, how low-dose methotrexate works is less clear." | Retrieved: Reviews: anti-inflammatory effect of low-dose methotrexate in RA, psoriasis, IBD is less clear; exact mechanism in RA uncertain.
claims.newSentence: In inflammatory conditions, how low-dose methotrexate works is less clear.

claims.evidence: Original: "Proposed explanations include effects on adenosine release, inflammatory signals and the growth of lymphocytes." | Retrieved: Review: proposed mechanisms include adenosine release, inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokines, suppression of lymphocyte proliferation; adenosine is the leading hypothesis.
claims.newSentence: Proposed explanations include effects on adenosine release, inflammatory signals and the growth of lymphocytes.

claims.evidence: Original: "Benefit builds slowly, and it can take weeks to months to feel the full effect." | Retrieved: NHS common questions: not a painkiller; may take up to 12 weeks to notice benefit and medicine is likely working in the meantime; Versus Arthritis similar.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says it can take a few months to notice any benefit, and that the medicine is likely to be working during that time.

claims.evidence: Original: "It is not a painkiller, although symptoms may ease as inflammation falls." | Retrieved: NHS: methotrexate is not a painkiller; pain may ease as inflammation falls.
claims.newSentence: It is not a painkiller, although there may be less pain as symptoms improve.

claims.evidence: Original: "It is available only on prescription." | Retrieved: NHS: available on prescription.
claims.newSentence: It is available only on prescription.

claims.evidence: Original: "Common side effects listed by the NHS include sensitivity to sunlight, ..." | Retrieved: NHS: skin may become very sensitive to sunlight.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says the skin may become very sensitive to sunlight.

claims.evidence: Original: "... loss of appetite, stomach upset, diarrhoea, headaches and tiredness." | Retrieved: Trust leaflets (OUH, GOSH): nausea/stomach upset, reduced appetite, diarrhoea, headache and tiredness are common; the NHS side-effects page text itself was not returned for this list.
claims.newSentence: Hospital leaflets list nausea or stomach upset, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache and tiredness among the more common side effects.

claims.evidence: Original: "Hair loss can happen and is usually not permanent." | Retrieved: NHS: hair loss unlikely to be permanent.
claims.newSentence: Hair loss can happen and is not likely to be permanent, according to the NHS.

claims.evidence: Original: "Folic acid is usually prescribed alongside it, because methotrexate can interfere with how the body takes up B vitamins." | Retrieved: Versus Arthritis: doctor will probably give folic acid tablets to help reduce unpleasant effects of the weekly methotrexate.
claims.newSentence: Versus Arthritis says folic acid tablets are usually prescribed to help reduce unpleasant effects of methotrexate.

claims.evidence: Original: "(new)" | Retrieved: NHS: serious side effects are rare.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says serious side effects are rare.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says to contact a doctor or NHS 111 about yellow skin or eyes, a persistent cough or breathlessness, leg swelling or urine changes." | Retrieved: NHS: yellow skin or eyes may be liver problems: call doctor or 111; persistent cough, chest pain, breathlessness may be lung inflammation: contact 111.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to contact a doctor or NHS 111 straight away about yellow skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, or a new cough, chest pain or breathlessness, which can be a sign of lung inflammation.

claims.evidence: Original: "... leg swelling or urine changes." | Retrieved: Leg swelling and urine changes were not found in retrieved NHS text.

Original: "The same list includes signs of infection and unexplained bruising or bleeding." | Retrieved: NHS: high temperature, aches or sore throat may be infection; bleeding gums, blood in urine, vomiting blood or unexplained bruising may be a blood disorder: contact doctor or 111.
claims.newSentence: The same NHS list includes signs of infection, such as a high temperature or sore throat, and signs of a blood problem, such as bleeding gums, blood in the urine or unexplained bruising.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says a severe allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing, needs a 999 call." | Retrieved: NHS: call 999 for lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swelling, fast or difficult breathing, collapse; do not drive yourself to A&E.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes fast or difficult.

claims.evidence: Original: "Methotrexate may increase the risk of liver or lung problems, particularly at high doses, which is why regular checks are done." | Retrieved: Versus Arthritis: methotrexate can affect the liver and cause the body to make fewer blood cells; regular blood tests catch this. 'Particularly at high doses' was not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: Versus Arthritis says methotrexate can affect the liver and lower the number of blood cells made, which is why regular blood tests are done.

claims.evidence: Original: "These include a patient card ... The MHRA materials say the card should be carried and shown ..." | Retrieved: MHRA: oral methotrexate for once-weekly use comes with a patient card to prompt weekly dosing; weekday is written on it; carry it and show unfamiliar clinicians; prescribers write the weekday in full.
claims.newSentence: The MHRA says oral methotrexate products used once weekly now come with a patient card that prompts weekly dosing, records the chosen weekday, and is carried to show clinicians who do not know the person's treatment.

claims.evidence: Original: "Prescribers are asked to write the weekday in full on the prescription, and pharmacists to write it on the card and the pack." | Retrieved: MHRA: the prescriber should specify the day of intake on the prescription, agreed with the patient and written in full.
claims.newSentence: Prescribers are asked to write the weekday in full on the prescription.

claims.evidence: Original: "... and pharmacists to write it on the card and the pack." | Retrieved: Pharmacists writing the weekday on card and pack was not confirmed in retrieved MHRA text.
Original: "In 2020 the MHRA introduced new measures to reduce the risk of fatal overdose from accidental daily dosing." | Retrieved: MHRA Drug Safety Update September 2020: new measures introduced.
claims.newSentence: In 2020 the MHRA introduced new measures to reduce the risk of fatal overdose from accidental daily dosing.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS lists allergy to methotrexate, severe liver or kidney disease, a blood disorder and current infection among reasons it may not be suitable." | Retrieved: NHS who-can-take page: not suitable with past allergic reaction, pregnancy or trying to conceive, breastfeeding, severe liver or kidney disease, a blood disorder, active infection; also mouth ulcers/stomach ulcers.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to methotrexate, severe liver or kidney disease, a blood disorder, an active infection, mouth or stomach ulcers, pregnancy and breastfeeding among reasons it may not be suitable.

claims.evidence: Original: "Because methotrexate affects the immune system, infections may be more likely." | Retrieved: NHS: may lower white blood cells, making infection more likely.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says methotrexate may lower the number of white cells in the blood, which can make infections more likely.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says to ask a doctor urgently about an infection, or after contact with someone who has chickenpox or shingles." | Retrieved: NHS common questions: ask doctor for urgent advice after contact with anyone who has chickenpox or shingles.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to ask a doctor for urgent advice after contact with someone who has chickenpox or shingles.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says methotrexate is not recommended in pregnancy, as it can cause birth defects. Anyone ... who wants to become pregnant is advised to speak to their doctor." | Retrieved: NHS pregnancy page: not recommended in pregnancy as it can cause birth defects; speak to doctor before trying to conceive.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says methotrexate is not recommended in pregnancy because it can cause birth defects, and advises speaking to a doctor before trying to get pregnant.

claims.evidence: Original: "If pregnancy happens during treatment, the NHS advises speaking to a doctor as soon as possible." | Retrieved: The 'speak to a doctor as soon as possible if pregnancy happens' sentence was not retrieved from the NHS page text.
Original: "(new, replaces father-exposure sentence)" | Retrieved: NHS: methotrexate may damage sperm in men and egg production in women.
claims.newSentence: The NHS pregnancy page says methotrexate may affect sperm in men and egg production in women.

claims.evidence: Original: "Shared-care protocols advise effective contraception during treatment and for some months afterwards, and the length of time differs between sources." | Retrieved: Several NHS shared-care documents and product information: effective contraception during treatment and for some months afterwards; length varies by source (3 vs 6 months).
claims.newSentence: NHS hospital guidance advises effective contraception during treatment and for some months afterwards, and the length of time differs between sources.

claims.evidence: Original: "Guidance on exposure through the father is less settled, so the specialist advises on timing." | Retrieved: Father-exposure advice is a local protocol/hospital leaflet matter, not stated by NHS or MHRA pages retrieved.

Original: "The NHS says that if methotrexate causes vomiting or severe diarrhoea, contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy." | Retrieved: Searches found nothing on vomiting or diarrhoea affecting contraceptive pills for methotrexate.

Original: "Breastfeeding is also listed among reasons methotrexate may not be suitable." | Retrieved: NHS who-can-take page lists breastfeeding as a reason it may not be suitable; NHS pregnancy page says tiny amounts pass into breast milk.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says tiny amounts of methotrexate pass into breast milk, and lists breastfeeding among situations where it may not be suitable.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says it is usually fine to drink alcohol with a low weekly dose, and to ask a doctor about higher doses." | Retrieved: NHS common questions: usually OK to drink alcohol on a low weekly dose; ask doctor if on a higher dose.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says it is usually fine to drink alcohol with a low weekly amount of methotrexate, and to ask a doctor if taking a higher amount.

claims.evidence: Original: "Live vaccines are avoided, while the NHS encourages other invited vaccinations and says to tell the person vaccinating about methotrexate." | Retrieved: SPS and hospital guidance: live vaccines are not recommended during treatment (e.g. yellow fever, MMR).
claims.newSentence: Live vaccines are not recommended during treatment.

claims.evidence: Original: "... the NHS encourages other invited vaccinations and says to tell the person vaccinating about methotrexate." | Retrieved: 'NHS encourages other invited vaccinations / tell the vaccinator' not found in retrieved NHS text (only trust FAQs on flu/pneumococcal).

Original: "NSAIDs ... can raise the risk of kidney toxicity with methotrexate, so they are used with caution on specialist advice." | Retrieved: SPS: NSAIDs with methotrexate can increase risk of methotrexate toxicity; some local guidance says NSAIDs can be continued with regular monitoring. 'Kidney toxicity' not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can increase the risk of methotrexate toxicity, so they are used only on specialist advice.

claims.evidence: Original: "Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole are advised against because of the risk of severe bone marrow suppression." | Retrieved: SPS and Scottish guidance: trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole interaction is severe; additive antifolate effect, bone marrow suppression; avoid.
claims.newSentence: Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole are advised against because of the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.

claims.evidence: Original: "Versus Arthritis says blood tests ... Tests are more frequent at the start and become less frequent once treatment is steady." | Retrieved: Versus Arthritis: blood tests before starting to check blood count, kidney and liver function; tests frequent at first, less often once stable. SPS lists FBC, liver and renal function at baseline.
claims.newSentence: Versus Arthritis says blood tests of the blood count, kidney function and liver function are needed before starting, are more frequent at first and become less frequent once treatment is steady.

claims.evidence: Original: "NHS monitoring guidance also lists ... a chest X-ray among the checks before starting." | Retrieved: NHS who-can-take page: a chest X-ray and breathing test may be done before starting.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a chest X-ray and breathing test may be done before starting.

claims.evidence: Original: "NHS monitoring guidance also lists hepatitis B and C and HIV screening ..." | Retrieved: SPS monitoring page lists hepatitis B in baseline checks. Hepatitis C and HIV screening not found in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service monitoring page lists hepatitis B among the checks before starting.

claims.evidence: Original: "The same guidance notes that a downward trend in results can point to toxicity even when values are still in range." | Retrieved: Downward trend can point to toxicity even in range: not found in retrieved text.

Original: "Brand names include Maxtrex for tablets, Metoject for pre-filled pens and Jylamvo for oral solution." | Retrieved: NHS methotrexate page lists UK brands Jylamvo, Maxtrex, Methofill, Metoject, Nordimet, Zlatal. Form pairings only in a local 2020 Sheffield protocol.
claims.newSentence: Brand names listed by the NHS include Jylamvo, Maxtrex, Methofill, Metoject, Nordimet and Zlatal.

claims.evidence: Original: "Xatmep (US brand); brand-form pairings" | Retrieved: Xatmep (US) was not retrieved from any source; brand/form pairings only in a local protocol.

Original: "Tablets, oral solution and pre-filled injection pens exist; for autoimmune conditions it is taken weekly, not daily." | Retrieved: NHS how-and-when: tablets and liquid with oral syringe; emc lists Metoject pens.
claims.newSentence: Methotrexate is available as tablets, an oral liquid and pre-filled injection pens, and for autoimmune conditions it is taken once a week, not daily.

claims.evidence: Original: "Class page repeat" | Retrieved: MHRA/NHS: weekly; oral products carry a patient card.
claims.newSentence: Taking methotrexate daily by mistake instead of weekly has caused overdoses that were sometimes fatal.

notes: Shared pool: 35 searches in total across the four items. The weekly-dosing warning is stated without any dose, citing MHRA (Sept 2020 DSU) and NHS; the MHRA patient card applies to oral products. Brand list is from the NHS page; brand-form pairings and Xatmep removed (only a local 2020 protocol / nothing). Removed: vomiting-and-contraceptive-pill, father exposure, NHS-encourages-vaccinations, 'pregnancy happens' advice, leg swelling/urine changes, downward-trend toxicity, HIV/hepatitis C screening, pharmacist-writes-on-pack, 'high doses' qualifier. Common side-effect list rests on hospital leaflets because the NHS side-effects page text was not fully returned (reworded accordingly). Breastfeeding: NHS who-can-take lists it as a reason for unsuitability while the NHS pregnancy page says tiny amounts pass into milk; the sentence reports both without a recommendation. NSAID wording: SPS says toxicity risk increased but a local protocol says NSAIDs can continue with monitoring. Live-vaccine sentence rests on SPS/hospital guidance. Aliases added (Methofill, Nordimet, Zlatal) - check for URL alias clashes. No dose, interval or cut-off in prose. Reused sentences count once.
